Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
make sure to stay close to exit
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
issues.explanation: This item is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the cognitive formulation. The active formulation is dominated by a Triggers–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Negative Appraisals inactive. In contrast, punishment/self-deserving-suffering is a negative self-appraisal theme rather than a threat-management strategy, and it does not connect plausibly to the selected trigger and threat items. The other maladaptive strategies (avoiding emotional stress, staying near exits) fit the trigger-threat-hypervigilance pattern, but punishment thinking pulls toward a different clinical profile that is otherwise not represented.

vignette: Mateo was thirty-two when the convoy rolled into the wadi. The IED detonation did not just shatter the armored frame; it threw him against the cab door, rattling his teeth and leaving a thick, metallic taste of copper and burnt dust coating his tongue. In the chaotic aftermath, as he pressed bandages into open wounds under the relentless sun, his balance failed, and a heavy wave of dizziness washed over him with every gasp. He survived the ambush, but the event left a permanent imprint on his nervous system. From that day forward, his mind operated on a single, unshakable premise: survival depended on knowing exactly where to run, and the environment itself was a predator waiting to strike. Over the following decades, that foundational fear calcified into a constant state of watchfulness. Because Mateo remained convinced that danger could materialize from a sudden noise at any moment, his hypervigilance never truly switched off. This relentless threat perception directly dictated his daily habits. He began systematically avoiding emotional conversations, terrified that feeling too deeply would compromise his survival reflexes, and he made a practice of staying anchored to an exit wherever he went. In his role as a special education teacher, this meant he no longer sat in the center of the staff room; he took the folding chair nearest the double doors, his body angled toward the hallway as if ready to bolt. The habit of checking his surroundings before stepping through any threshold became so rigid that it isolated him from former colleagues, who slowly stopped inviting him to faculty dinners or weekend trips. The classroom environment soon became a minefield that fed his fear system in a tightly wound sequence. During an IEP planning session, a colleague’s loud laugh from across the table sent his pulse hammering, and the mere thought of recounting his military service during veteran appreciation week ignited a flare of panic. Both the sudden auditory shock and the prospect of event recall instantly amplified his threat assessment, making him certain he was being judged for any sign of weakness. Because he was constantly scanning for danger, his physical sensitivity sharpened; a slight drop in blood pressure while grading papers triggered a fresh wave of dizziness, which in turn became a potent reminder of the wadi, making the taste of copper and the tilt of the floor suddenly overwhelming. He quietly excused himself, slipping out to the parking lot to ground himself, knowing that only by avoiding the emotional weight of the room and checking his escape path could he keep the panic at bay. By continuously steering clear of emotional stress and constantly verifying that doors were unobstructed, he denied his brain the chance to relearn safety, and his threat perception only intensified, locking his hypervigilance and escape route planning into an unbreakable loop. Now at sixty-five, Mateo found that the careful architecture of his avoidance was finally collapsing under the weight of exhaustion. The dizziness no longer stayed confined to his classroom; it followed him to the grocery store and his quiet apartment, making him question whether he was suffering from a heart condition or simply his own relentless vigilance. He sat in the intake office today, his hands resting on his knees, acutely aware of the clock on the wall and the precise location of the reception desk’s side door. He had finally made the call because the silence in his own head had grown too loud to bear. He hoped someone could help him unclench the grip that had kept him alive in the desert but was now suffocating the rest of his years, though he worried, more than anything, that letting go of his watchfulness would leave him defenseless against a threat he could no longer outrun.
